Valmiki and Narada

Stories of the Ramayana

Valmiki and Narada

The First Shloka

In plain English — how the Ramayana came to be

Stories by Eku

How to Read This Book · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it aloud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting with everyone at home.

In the yellow boxes, the characters speak in their own words. Change your voice a little as you read them — Narada sweet, Valmiki grave, Brahma calm.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of each part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listener speak. This story begins with a question — and thinking about questions is its real lesson.

This is the first story of the Ramayana — the story that comes before the Ramayana. It does not tell Rama's whole tale; it tells how the Ramayana came to be. Rama's great story will be told in its own books.

The main story of this book comes from Valmiki's Ramayana, Balakanda, sargas 1–4. Where other traditions tell the tale a little differently, that is given separately at the end, under Where This Story Comes From — nothing has been mixed into the main story.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Valmiki — the heart of this story. A great sage (rishi) living in the forest, an ascetic and a master of the Vedas. The world calls him the Adi Kavi, the first poet — because the first verse (shloka) came from his lips.

Narada — the divine sage (Devarshi), sage among the gods. A veena in his hand, wandering through all three worlds, knowing everything. Valmiki asks him his question.

Bharadwaja — Valmiki's disciple. He walks with his teacher to the Tamasa river and is amazed at the words he hears.

Brahma — the creator, the four-faced god. He comes to Valmiki and commands him to compose the Ramayana.

Rama — the prince of Ayodhya, of the Ikshvaku line. He does not appear in person in this book — Narada tells his story, and hearing it, Valmiki writes the Ramayana.

The krauncha pair — two sarus cranes on the bank of the Tamasa, male and female, always together. Seeing them, grief rose in Valmiki's heart — and from that grief came the first shloka.

The Nishada hunter — a forest hunter, who shot an arrow at the krauncha bird.

Lava and Kusha — Rama's two sons. They grew up in Valmiki's hermitage, learned the Ramayana from him, and sang it to the world.

1 · The Sage's Question · · THE SAGE'S QUESTION

Long, long ago, there was a quiet hermitage in the middle of a forest, where the sage Valmiki lived. He was an ascetic, a knower of the Vedas, and counted the greatest master of speech.

One day a special guest came to his hermitage — the divine sage Narada. A veena in his hand, a smile on his face, carrying news of all three worlds. Wherever Narada went, a story began on its own.

Valmiki welcomed Narada — gave him a seat, water, and fruit. Then he sat down and asked the question that had been in his heart for many days.

Valmiki asked: “Narada, tell me — who is there in this world today in whom all virtues live together? One who is virtuous and also brave; who knows dharma and speaks the truth; who is grateful — never forgetting a kindness done to him; whose vow is unbreakable; whose character is an example for all; who wishes well to every living being; who is learned and also humble; who has conquered anger and whose fame has spread far and wide?”

This was no small question. Valmiki was naming sixteen qualities — together, in a single human being. To find such a person is very hard.

Narada smiled. He knew the answer to this question.

Narada said: “Great sage, what you have asked is very rare — but such a man exists. He lives in this very world, right now. His name is — Rama.”

Pause and think — Valmiki did not ask for wealth, or a kingdom, or a boon. He asked — what is a good human being like? Does that question ever rise in our hearts too — what does a good person look like? And do we look for its answer around us?

2 · Narada Tells Rama's Story · · NARADA TELLS RAMA'S STORY

Narada said — Rama is the son of King Dasharatha of Ayodhya, of the Ikshvaku line. He holds all sixteen qualities you named — and more.

Then Narada told Rama's whole story in brief — as if pouring a great river into a single pot.

He told how Rama went into fourteen years of forest exile on his father's word; how his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana went with him; how he fought demons in the forest; how Ravana carried Sita away to Lanka; how Rama befriended the monkeys, built a bridge across the sea, defeated Ravana and brought Sita back; and how he returned to Ayodhya and became king.

As he listened, a picture of Rama formed in Valmiki's mind — bow in hand, walking the forest path, with Sita and Lakshmana, among the monkeys, standing before Lanka.

And at the end of the story Narada said — whoever hears this story of Rama, reads it, or tells it, their heart will be purified, their home will be happy, and they will find the path of dharma. Rama's story is not only a story — it is a way of living.

Narada said: “Great sage, this is the man you were looking for. Now you know — who Rama is.”

Saying this, Narada bowed to Valmiki, lifted his veena — and walked toward the sky. Valmiki stood at the door of the hermitage, watching him go.

Rama's story was now in his heart — but it was only heard, not yet written. The time to write had not yet come.

Pause and think — Narada told Rama's whole story in a short while — from birth to kingship. But Valmiki did not start writing at once. Is a story ever written the moment it is heard — or does it first need time to live, ripen and grow in the heart? Which story that you heard still lives in your heart?

3 · By the Tamasa River · · BY THE TAMASA RIVER

A short while after Narada left, Valmiki set out with his disciple Bharadwaja to bathe. Near the hermitage flowed a river — the Tamasa.

The water of the Tamasa was so clear that you could see right to the bottom. Valmiki stopped and said to his disciple —

Valmiki said: “Bharadwaja, look — how pure this water is, like the mind of a good man. Today I shall bathe here.”

On the riverbank, on the green grass, sat a pair of krauncha birds — male and female. Kraunchas are tall, beautiful birds like sarus cranes, who stay together for life. The two were wandering side by side, calling in sweet voices, close to each other.

Valmiki was glad to see them. Such a sight in the forest — peace, love and togetherness — whose heart would it not fill?

Then, without any warning, a Nishada hunter stepped out from behind the bushes. He raised his bow, fitted an arrow — and let it fly at the male krauncha.

(Pause here, then speak very softly) The male bird fell on the grass. The female bird did not fly away — she circled above her mate, and her cry of grief echoed through the forest.

What rose in Valmiki's heart was, before anger, grief — for an innocent creature, for a broken pair, for a pain that had no cause.

Pause and think — The water of the Tamasa was pure, like the mind of a good man — and on that very bank, grief suddenly arrived. Do peace and grief live side by side like this? Valmiki first felt gladness at seeing the birds, then grief — can one sight stir two feelings in our hearts at once?

4 · The First Shloka, Born of Grief · · THE FIRST SHLOKA

Valmiki kept looking at the hunter. The grief in his heart was so deep that it poured out in words — without thinking, without counting, on its own.

What came from his lips was no ordinary speech. The words bound themselves into a metre on their own — four parts, eight syllables in each part, a rhythm, a beat.

Hunter, may you never find a lasting home
or peace of mind for endless years —
for you struck down one of a loving pair
of cranes, lost in love.

These were the words of the first verse. In Sanskrit they are — “Ma nishada pratishtham tvam agamah shashvatih samah, yat kraunca-mithunad ekam avadhih kama-mohitam.” Their plain meaning is: “O hunter! May you never attain steadiness or peace for endless years — because you killed one of a pair of kraunchas lost in love.”

Valmiki himself was amazed. He said to Bharadwaja — “Look at what came from my lips! This speech born of grief has bound itself into a metre on its own.”

Bharadwaja bowed his head and said — “Teacher, this is no ordinary speech. This is a shloka.”

They say shloka (verse) was born from shoka (grief) — the first metre was born from sorrow. The grief that rose in Valmiki's heart became the rhythm of words. And that rhythm was the Anushtubh metre, in which the whole Ramayana would one day be written.

Valmiki said: “Bharadwaja, these words have not left my heart — they still echo in my ears. There is something in them — something great.”

Pause and think — Grief made Valmiki a poet — from shoka came shloka. Does grief only break things — or can it sometimes make something new? When we feel grief for someone, does that grief move us to say something, do something, or change something?

5 · Brahma's Command · · BRAHMA'S COMMAND

Valmiki was still speaking of this with his disciple when a divine light spread across the sky. Brahma — the creator, the four-faced god — arrived there on his swan.

Valmiki rose and welcomed him — gave him a seat, offered water, bowed low. Brahma smiled and said —

Brahma said: “Valmiki, what came from your lips is no ordinary speech — it is a shloka, in the Anushtubh metre. This happened by my own will. Now write Rama's story in this very metre — the same story that Narada told you.”

Brahma said — let nothing in Rama's story be left out, and let nothing in it be false. Write what Narada told you — and what you see in meditation, write that too. This story will live for ages.

Saying this, Brahma returned to his own world. Valmiki sat in the hermitage — and now a great task lay before him.

Valmiki sat in meditation. And in meditation, Rama's whole story began to appear before him — as if a river were flowing past. The palace of Ayodhya, Dasharatha's sacrifice, the birth of the four sons, the forest journey with Vishwamitra, the breaking of the bow, the wedding with Sita, the exile, the war in Lanka, and the return to Ayodhya — scene after scene, word after word.

And he began to write — in the same metre that had come from his grief on the bank of the Tamasa. Verse after verse, sarga after sarga. Tradition says the whole Ramayana came to twenty-four thousand shlokas, five hundred sargas and seven kandas — Balakanda, Ayodhyakanda, Aranyakanda, Kishkindhakanda, Sundarakanda, Yuddhakanda and Uttarakanda.

And so a story that began with a hunter's arrow — with a shloka born from a bird's grief — became one of the greatest stories in the world.

Pause and think — Brahma told Valmiki — write what Narada told you, and what you see in meditation, write that too. Is writing only the work of listening — or also of seeing and feeling in the heart? Valmiki first had to hear the story, then feel the grief, before he could write. Do great stories come to be like this — by hearing, feeling, and then writing?

6 · Lava and Kusha Sing · · LAVA AND KUSHA SING

When the Ramayana was complete, Valmiki thought — to whom shall I teach this story now? A story lives only when someone sings it, when someone tells it.

At that time two boys lived in his hermitage — Lava and Kusha, Rama's two sons. They had grown up in the hermitage, they were Valmiki's disciples, and they sang very sweetly.

Valmiki taught the whole Ramayana to Lava and Kusha — verse after verse, sarga after sarga. The two boys learned it by heart, as if it were their own story.

Then one day the two boys went to Ayodhya — and there they sang the Ramayana. To the tune of the veena, in sweet voices, Rama's own story — before Rama himself.

Rama heard them — and was amazed. This story was his own! He called the boys to court, honoured them, and heard the whole story from them.

The story says Rama then knew that Valmiki had written this tale — the same Valmiki in whose hermitage Sita lived, and whose disciples these two boys were.

And so the Ramayana travelled out of the hermitage and spread through the world — on one boy's veena, on another boy's voice, and from the first shloka born of a sage's grief.

A story that began with a question, bound in a shloka born of grief —
and carried to the world by the song of two boys.

Pause and think — Valmiki wrote the Ramayana — but it reached the world through the song of Lava and Kusha. Is a story only complete when someone sings it and someone hears it? Which story in your home is passed on by singing or telling — and who will pass it on next?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

This book is the first story of the Ramayana — and it teaches us three things.

First — asking questions. Valmiki asked — what is a good human being like? And from that question the Ramayana began. One who never asks a question never receives an answer.

Second — seeing grief. Valmiki saw the krauncha's grief, felt it — and from that grief came the first shloka. One who does not see another's grief cannot become a poet — nor a complete human being.

Third — passing the story on. Valmiki wrote, Lava and Kusha sang, Rama listened — and so the story lived for ages.

Ask the listeners:

1. Valmiki named sixteen qualities — virtuous, brave, knower of dharma, truthful, grateful, firm in vow, of noble character, wishing well to all. Which of these qualities feels hardest to you — and why?

2. Narada told Rama's whole story in brief — and Valmiki did not write it at once. Why does a story need time to ripen in the heart?

3. The water of the Tamasa was pure, like the mind of a good man. What should we do to keep our own minds pure?

4. From shoka came shloka — from grief came verse. Can grief ever make something good? Remember a moment like that from your own life.

5. Brahma said — write what Narada told you, just as it is. Should truth be written exactly as it is — or dressed up and decorated?

6. Lava and Kusha sang the Ramayana, and only then did it reach the world. Which story of your home would you like to pass on?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book comes from Valmiki's Ramayana, Balakanda, sargas 1–4 — in sarga 1, Valmiki's question to Narada and Narada's brief telling of Rama's story; in sarga 2, the Tamasa river, the krauncha pair, the hunter's arrow, the first shloka and the arrival of Brahma; in sargas 3–4, the composing of the Ramayana and its teaching to Lava and Kusha.

The Sixteen Qualities — the Question

Valmiki asked Narada about a man with sixteen qualities — gunavan (virtuous), viryavan (brave), dharmajna (knower of dharma), kritajna (grateful), satyavakya (truthful in speech), dridhavrata (firm in vow), charitravan (of noble character), sarvabhuta-hita (wishing well to all beings), and others like them. In this book the qualities are named in plain words, not as a translation of the verse.

The First Shloka

The first shloka is Balakanda 2.15 — “Ma nishada pratishtham tvam agamah shashvatih samah, yat kraunca-mithunad ekam avadhih kama-mohitam” — an ancient public-domain text, given in this book in plain meaning. Tradition says the verse is in the Anushtubh metre — four quarters, eight syllables in each — and that shloka was born from shoka (grief).

The Krauncha Bird

Krauchas are birds like sarus cranes, who stay together for life — which is why the killing of one of the pair was so full of grief. In Valmiki's text the female bird is shown wailing beside her mate; this book does not say that she died, because that is not in Valmiki's text.

The Robber Story — a Later Tradition

There is a famous story about Valmiki's earlier life — that he was once a robber, met Narada, and became a sage through penance. That story is not in Balakanda 1–4; it belongs to a later tradition. That is why it is not in the main story here — in the Ramayana, Valmiki appears only as an ascetic sage.

Lava and Kusha Singing — Uttarakanda

Lava and Kusha singing the Ramayana in Ayodhya, and Rama hearing them — that story belongs to the Uttarakanda, not the Balakanda. It is kept here in brief, to complete the journey of the Ramayana, and its source is named separately here.

Twenty-Four Thousand Shlokas

Twenty-four thousand shlokas, five hundred sargas and seven kandas — this is the traditional count of the Ramayana, handed down from the epic's own description. Different manuscripts may differ slightly in the number of verses.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of how the Ramayana was made comes to rest — but Rama's story has not even begun. In the books that follow, the same tale will be told that Narada told in brief — from Ayodhya to the forest, from the forest to Lanka, and from Lanka back to Ayodhya.

And whenever grief at another's pain rises in your heart, remember the bank of the Tamasa — where a sage's grief gave birth to the first shloka.

— The End —
